summary: Describes requirements and mechanisms for telling a traffic-engineered MPLS or GMPLS network that a link or router will soon be turned off. The aim is to cut or avoid traffic disruption during planned maintenance. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes how a network operator takes a traffic-engineered link out of service without dropping the traffic on it. The operator first tells the rest of the network that the link is going away, waits while the traffic moves elsewhere, and only then switches the link off.

questions: how to shut down a te link without traffic loss
what is graceful shutdown in mpls
how to shut down mpls link without traffic loss
subtitle: Telling the network a link is about to go away, so traffic can be moved first.

tldr.problem: A provider that takes a traffic-engineered link or router out of service for maintenance causes traffic disruption, and unlike a failure there is no recovery mechanism to absorb it.
tldr.mechanism: The document splits the shutdown into two steps: the control plane is told first, by advertising the link as having no bandwidth and by sending RSVP-TE PathErr notifications, and the data plane is disabled later, after a delay that lets traffic move.
tldr.outcome: The requirements and mechanisms are given for a single link, a link inside a bundle, a label resource, a set of links and a whole node, for both MPLS-TE and its GMPLS extensions.

facts.label: Trap generated for a shut down link

today: RFC 5817 is an Informational document published by the IETF in April 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It sets out requirements and mechanisms for a planned shutdown in MPLS-TE and GMPLS networks, and states that it introduces no new security considerations of its own.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
When outages in a network are planned, for maintenance for example, mechanisms can be used to avoid traffic disruption. This is different from unplanned element failure, where traffic disruption can be minimised by recovery mechanisms but may not be avoided. A service provider may therefore want to remove a traffic-engineered link, a group of links or an entire node temporarily or indefinitely, for reasons such as link maintenance, a software or hardware upgrade at a node, or significant traffic engineering configuration changes. In all of these cases the goal is to minimise the impact on the traffic carried over traffic-engineered label switched paths by triggering notifications so that the flows are rerouted gracefully before the administrative procedures start.

The operations described apply equally to MPLS-TE and to its Generalized MPLS extensions. The document describes graceful shutdown of a resource such as a traffic-engineered link, a component link inside a bundled link, a label resource or an entire traffic-engineered node.

Graceful shutdown may take several steps, divided into two sets: disabling the resource in the control plane and disabling it in the data plane. The node that starts the shutdown introduces a delay between the two sets, so that the control plane has time to divert traffic away from the resource. The trigger for the event is a local matter at the node that starts it, and graceful shutdown is typically triggered for administrative reasons such as link maintenance or an upgrade.
sections.plainLanguage: A planned shutdown has two parts. The network is first told that the link is going away, and traffic is moved elsewhere. Only after a pause is the link actually switched off, so that nothing is dropped.

sections.title: Requirements for Graceful Shutdown
sections.content:
The requirements cover graceful removal of one traffic-engineered link, one component link within a bundled link, a set of links, a set of component links, label resources, or an entire node.

Once an operator has started the shutdown of a resource, no new traffic-engineered path may be set up that uses it. Any signalling message for a new path that explicitly specifies the resource, or that would need it because of local constraints, is required to be rejected as if the resource were unavailable. It is desirable for such set-up attempts to avoid the resource altogether by selecting an alternate route or other resources.

If the resource being shut down is the last-resort resource for reaching a destination from a given head-end node, then the node that started the shutdown can cancel the operation, based on a local decision. The ingress node must be given the opportunity to take actions that reduce or eliminate traffic disruption on the paths using the resources that are about to be shut down.

The mechanisms are equally applicable to paths inside one domain and to paths spanning multiple domains, such as IGP areas and autonomous systems, and to packet and non-packet networks. For rerouting to work, a node that starts the shutdown has to notify all the other network nodes about the resource under shutdown. Depending on the switching technology it may also be possible to shut down a label resource, for example one lambda in a lambda switch capable node.
sections.plainLanguage: While a resource is being closed, new paths must not be set up over it, and the nodes at the ends of the affected paths must be told so that they can build new paths. If there is no other way to reach a destination, the operator's node can call the whole thing off.

sections.title: OSPF and IS-IS Notification
sections.content:
An approach based only on the interior gateway protocols is not applicable to inter-area and inter-autonomous-system traffic engineering, because IGP flooding is restricted to IGP areas and levels. The document therefore uses RSVP signalling for paths that span multiple domains, and uses existing IGP mechanisms for the shutdown notification, which discourages nodes from setting up new paths over the resources being shut down. A node where a link or the whole node is being shut down first triggers the IGP updates, and then, after a delay that allows the network to converge, uses the RSVP signalling.

The OSPF and IS-IS procedures are similar to the graceful restart procedures of those protocols. The node where the shutdown of a link is wanted originates the traffic engineering LSA or IS-IS LSP containing a Link TLV for the link under shutdown, with the traffic engineering metric set to 0xffffffff, that is, 0 as unreserved bandwidth. If the link has a lambda or fibre switching capability, it also has 0 in the maximum LSP bandwidth field of the Interface Switching Capability Descriptor sub-TLV. A node may also specify a value greater than the available bandwidth in the minimum LSP bandwidth field of the same sub-TLV, which discourages new path establishment through the link.

If the shutdown covers a component link inside a bundle and it is not the last component link available, the link attributes for the bundle are recomputed, and the same is done when a label resource inside a link is shut down. If that removal causes a significant bandwidth change event, a new LSA is originated with the new traffic parameters. If the last component link is being shut down, the routing procedure for link removal is used instead. Neighbours of the node where the shutdown is in progress continue to advertise the actual unreserved bandwidth of their links to that node, without any routing adjacency change. A node-level shutdown follows the same procedure for all of its traffic-engineered links.
sections.plainLanguage: The first step uses the routing protocol the network already runs. The node advertises the link as having no bandwidth left, so every router in the area stops sending new traffic over it and can plan a different path.

sections.title: RSVP-TE Signalling and Rerouting
sections.content:
The signalling part of the shutdown uses the TE LSP rerouting mechanism defined in RFC 5710. A node where the shutdown of an unbundled link or of an entire bundled link is wanted triggers a PathErr message with the error code Notify and the error value Local link maintenance required, for all affected paths. A node that is itself being shut down triggers a PathErr with the error code Notify and the error value Local node maintenance required, for all paths. The PathErr message may carry either an RFC 2205 format ERROR_SPEC object or an IF_ID format one, and it is the address and TLVs carried by that object, not the error value, that indicate which resource is being shut down.

Shutting down one component link of a bundle is different, because a path is pinned to a component link, and the remaining component links may still admit new paths. The node triggers a PathErr with the error code Notify and the error value Local link maintenance required, and builds the rest of the ERROR_SPEC object using the component reroute request procedure. Shutting down a label resource uses the error code and value Notify with Local link maintenance required, and the label reroute request procedure.

When a head-end node, a transit node or a border node receives one of these PathErr messages, it follows the procedures of RFC 5710 to reroute the traffic around the resource. When it computes the new path it avoids the resources named in the ERROR_SPEC object. If a Path Computation Element does the computation, the node acting as its client states in the request that the computation should avoid the resource. How long the node keeps avoiding the resource is a local decision.

If the node that started the shutdown receives a path setup request for a new tunnel that would use the resource, it answers with a PathErr carrying the Notify code and an error value consistent with the type of resource. If the resource is the last-resort resource for a destination, the node can cancel the shutdown instead. The node can also delay the actual removal of the resource from forwarding, following the reroute request timeout procedure, which gives the network time to move traffic away. New and existing tunnels are told apart by inspecting the sender template and session objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The second step uses the signalling that already sets up traffic-engineered paths. The node that is closing the link sends a message to the paths affected, naming the link or node being closed, and the far end of each path then works out a new route that avoids it.

sections.title: Manageability Considerations
sections.content: When a traffic-engineered link is being shut down, a linkDown trap as defined in RFC 2863 should be generated for that link. When a bundled link is being shut down, a linkDown trap should be generated for the bundled link and for each of its component links. When a traffic-engineered node is being shut down, a linkDown trap should be generated for all of the traffic-engineered links at that node.
sections.plainLanguage: The management system is told about the shutdown the same way it is told about a broken link, so that the usual monitoring reacts in the usual way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces no new security considerations, because it describes the use of existing formats and mechanisms. It relies on the existing procedures for advertising traffic engineering LSAs and IS-IS LSPs containing Link TLVs. Tampering with those advertisements may affect traffic engineering computations, and the memo suggests that any mechanisms used to secure the transmission of normal LSAs and IS-IS LSPs be applied equally to the opaque LSAs and IS-IS LSPs this document uses. The security considerations given in RFC 3630, RFC 5305, RFC 4203 and RFC 5307 remain relevant and sufficient, together with the security considerations of RFC 5710 and Section 9 of RFC 4736.
sections.plainLanguage: No new security rules are introduced, because the shutdown reuses messages that already exist. The existing rules for protecting routing advertisements apply to these messages too.

viz.caption: THE TWO STAGES OF A GRACEFUL SHUTDOWN

messages.label: IGP UPDATE
messages.note: The link is advertised with the traffic engineering metric set to 0xffffffff, so no new path is built over it.

messages.label: PATH COMPUTATION
messages.note: The network converges on paths that avoid the link.

messages.label: PATHERR NOTIFY
messages.note: The affected paths are told that local link maintenance is required, naming the resource in the ERROR_SPEC object.

messages.label: NEW PATH
messages.note: The head-end signals a replacement path that avoids the resource, and the old path is torn down.

viz.caption: THE PATHERR NOTIFICATIONS USED FOR GRACEFUL SHUTDOWN

items.label: Link shutdown
items.desc: Sent for an unbundled link, a bundle, or a component link inside a bundle that is not the last one.

items.label: Node shutdown
items.desc: Sent for all paths when the node itself is being shut down.

items.label: Resource identification
items.desc: The address and TLVs in the object name the resource to be shut down.

items.label: Alternative object format
items.desc: The GMPLS interface identifier form of the same object may be used instead.
